'''Cyclic glycine-proline''' ('''cGP''') is a small [[neuroactive peptide]] that belongs to a group of bioactive [[2,5-diketopiperazine]]s (2,5-DKPs) and is also known as cyclo-glycine-proline. cGP is a neutral, stable naturally occurring compound and is endogenous to the human body; found in human plasma, breast milk and cerebrospinal fluid.  DKPs are bioactive compounds often found in foods. Cyclic dipeptides such as 2,5 DKPs are formed by the cyclisation of two amino acids of linear peptides produced in heated or fermented foods.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Otsuka Y, Arita H, Sakaji M, Yamamoto K, Kashiwagi T, Shimamura T, Ukeda H | title = Investigation of the formation mechanism of proline-containing cyclic dipeptide from the linear peptide | journal = Bioscience, Biotechnology, and Biochemistry | volume = 83 | issue = 12 | pages = 2355–2363 | date = December 2019 | pmid = 31462170 | doi = 10.1080/09168451.2019.1659718 | s2cid = 201663846 | doi-access = free }}</ref> The bioactivity of cGP is a property of [[functional food]]s and presents in several matrices of foods including blackcurrants.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fan D, Alamri Y, Liu K, MacAskill M, Harris P, Brimble M, Dalrymple-Alford J, Prickett T, Menzies O, Laurenson A, Anderson T, Guan J | title = Supplementation of Blackcurrant Anthocyanins Increased Cyclic Glycine-Proline in the Cerebrospinal Fluid of Parkinson Patients: Potential Treatment to Improve Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1 Function | journal = Nutrients | volume = 10 | issue = 6 | page = 714 | date = June 2018 | pmid = 29865234 | pmc = 6024688 | doi = 10.3390/nu10060714 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

cGP is metabolite of hormone insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). It has a cyclic structure, lipophilic nature, and is enzymatically stable which makes its a more favorable candidate for manipulating the binding-release process between IGF-1 and its binding protein thereby, normalizing IGF-1 function.<ref name="LTran-patent-7232798">{{cite patent | inventor = Tran LH | country = US | number = 7232798 | url = https://patents.google.com/patent/US7232798B2/en?oq=US7232798 | title = Neuroprotection and neurogenesis by administering cyclic prolyl glycine | gdate = 19 June 2007 | assign = NeuroBioMed Corp.}}</ref>

Under the trade name '''Traneurocin''' (developmental code name '''NA-831'''), it is being developed as a [[racetam]]-like [[drug]] for the treatment of [[COVID-19]], [[Alzheimer's disease]], [[fragile X syndrome]], [[Rett syndrome]], [[major depressive disorder]], and other [[neurological disorder]]s.<ref name="AdisInsight">{{cite web | title=Traneurocin | work = AdisInsight | publisher = Springer Nature Switzerland AG | date=25 September 2024 | url=https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800051889 | access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref><ref name="Synapse">{{cite web | title=Delving into the Latest Updates on Traneurocin with Synapse | website=Synapse | date=19 September 2024 | url=https://synapse.patsnap.com/drug/c500c569063d4c70af222dab403c0593 | access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref><ref name="GudashevaGrigorievKoliasnikova2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gudasheva TA, Grigoriev VV, Koliasnikova KN, Zamoyski VL, Seredenin SB | title = Neuropeptide cycloprolylglycine is an endogenous positive modulator of AMPA receptors | journal = Doklady. Biochemistry and Biophysics | volume = 471 | issue = 1 | pages = 387–389 | date = November 2016 | pmid = 28058675 | doi = 10.1134/S160767291606003X }}</ref> In the case of COVID-19, it is specifically being developed for treatment of COVID-19-induced [[neuropathy]].<ref name="ChoiChoiKopp2024" />

== Endogenous synthesis ==
[[Insulin-like growth factor 1]] (IGF-1) is a hormone that is structurally very similar to insulin and mediates the effects of [[growth hormone]] (GH) thus affecting metabolism, regeneration, and overall development.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Laron Z | title = Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1): a growth hormone | journal = Molecular Pathology | volume = 54 | issue = 5 | pages = 311–316 | date = October 2001 | pmid = 11577173 | pmc = 1187088 | doi = 10.1136/mp.54.5.311 }}</ref> The GH-IGF-1 signaling pathway is crucial in the process of vascular remodeling and angiogenesis, i.e., the process of building new blood vessels and thus, helps in maintaining blood circulation in the body.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lin S, Zhang Q, Shao X, Zhang T, Xue C, Shi S, Zhao D, Lin Y | title = IGF-1 promotes angiogenesis in endothelial cells/adipose-derived stem cells co-culture system with activation of PI3K/Akt signal pathway | journal = Cell Proliferation | volume = 50 | issue = 6 | date = December 2017 | article-number = e12390 | pmid = 28960620 | pmc = 6529130 | doi = 10.1111/cpr.12390 | s2cid = 8857741 }}</ref><ref name="Age-related memory decline is assoc">{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhang R, Kadar T, Sirimanne E, MacGibbon A, Guan J | title = Age-related memory decline is associated with vascular and microglial degeneration in aged rats | journal = Behavioural Brain Research | volume = 235 | issue = 2 | pages = 210–217 | date = December 2012 | pmid = 22889927 | doi = 10.1016/j.bbr.2012.08.002 | s2cid = 22501566 }}</ref> In the brain, IGF-1 is abundant in various cells and regions and research over the years, suggest an imperative role of IGF-1 activity in neurodevelopment making it critical in learning and memory.<ref name="Guan Harris Brimble et al 2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Guan J, Harris P, Brimble M, Lei Y, Lu J, Yang Y, Gunn AJ | title = The role for IGF-1-derived small neuropeptides as a therapeutic target for neurological disorders | journal = Expert Opinion on Therapeutic Targets | volume = 19 | issue = 6 | pages = 785–793 | date = June 2015 | pmid = 25652713 | doi = 10.1517/14728222.2015.1010514 | s2cid = 19257181 }}</ref>

The IGF-1 family comprises
* IGF-1,
* IGF receptors (IGF-1R) and
* IGF binding proteins (IGFBP).

The therapeutic applications of IGF-1 are limited due to its poor central uptake and potential side-effects. IGF-1 that is not bound to its binding protein bears a very short half-life and is cleaved by enzymes to form the tripeptide glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE). However, the enzymatic instability of GPE, with a plasma half-life of less than 4 minutes, is further cleaved to produce the final product, cyclic-Glycine-Proline (cGP).<ref name="LTran-patent-7232798"/><ref name="Guan Harris Brimble et al 2015"/><ref name="Shanmugalingam Bosco Ridley et al 2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Shanmugalingam T, Bosco C, Ridley AJ, Van Hemelrijck M | title = Is there a role for IGF-1 in the development of second primary cancers? | journal = Cancer Medicine | volume = 5 | issue = 11 | pages = 3353–3367 | date = November 2016 | pmid = 27734632 | pmc = 5119990 | doi = 10.1002/cam4.871 }}</ref>

== Biological Role of cGP ==
The hepatic production of IGF-1 is controlled by the growth hormone (GH)-IGF-1 axis.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bianchi VE, Locatelli V, Rizzi L | title = Neurotrophic and Neuroregenerative Effects of GH/IGF1 | journal = International Journal of Molecular Sciences | volume = 18 | issue = 11 | page = 2441 | date = November 2017 | pmid = 29149058 | pmc = 5713408 | doi = 10.3390/ijms18112441 | doi-access = free }}</ref> The majority of circulating IGF-1 is not bioavailable because of its affinity and binding to IGF-binding protein (IGFBP), mainly IGFBP3. IGF-1 bioactivity is therefore, tightly regulated through reversible binding with IGFBP3.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sara VR, Hall K | title = Insulin-like growth factors and their binding proteins | journal = Physiological Reviews | volume = 70 | issue = 3 | pages = 591–614 | date = July 1990 | pmid = 1694588 | doi = 10.1152/physrev.1990.70.3.591 | bibcode = 1990PhyRv..70..591S }}</ref> It is this binding-release process that determines the amount of bioavailable IGF-1 in circulation. IGF-1 that is not bound, is cleaved into an N-terminal tripeptide, glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE) and Des-N-IGF-1.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yamamoto H, Murphy LJ | title = Generation of des-(1-3) insulin-like growth factor-I in serum by an acid protease | journal = Endocrinology | volume = 135 | issue = 6 | pages = 2432–2439 | date = December 1994 | pmid = 7988428 | doi = 10.1210/endo.135.6.7988428 }}</ref> and GPE metabolizes to result in cyclic glycine proline (cGP).<ref name="LTran-patent-7232798"/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Samonina G, Ashmarin I, Lyapina L | title = Glyproline peptide family: review on bioactivity and possible origins | journal = Pathophysiology | volume = 8 | issue = 4 | pages = 229–234 | date = August 2002 | pmid = 12100966 | doi = 10.1016/S0928-4680(02)00018-4 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Unbound IGF-1, cleaved at the N-terminal, can be metabolized through a series of downstream enzymatic reactions to cGP. The N-terminal is the binding site of IGF-1 which allows cGP to retain the same binding affinity to IGFBP-3 and thus, regulates the bioavailability of IGF-1 through competitive binding with IGFBP3. An increase in cGP, would increase competitive advantage and thus, increase the amount of circulating and therefore, bioavailable IGF-1.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fan D, Krishnamurthi R, Harris P, Barber PA, Guan J | title = Plasma cyclic glycine proline/IGF-1 ratio predicts clinical outcome and recovery in stroke patients | journal = Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology | volume = 6 | issue = 4 | pages = 669–677 | date = April 2019 | pmid = 31019991 | pmc = 6469247 | doi = 10.1002/acn3.743 | s2cid = 104430959 }}</ref><ref name="Fan Pitcher Dalrymple‐Alford et al 2020">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fan D, Pitcher T, Dalrymple-Alford J, MacAskill M, Anderson T, Guan J | title = Changes of plasma cGP/IGF-1 molar ratio with age is associated with cognitive status of Parkinson disease | journal = Alzheimer's & Dementia | volume = 12 | issue = 1 | article-number = e12025 | date = January 2020 | pmid = 32671179 | pmc = 7346731 | doi = 10.1002/dad2.12025 }}</ref><ref name="Guan Gluckman Yang et al 2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Guan J, Gluckman P, Yang P, Krissansen G, Sun X, Zhou Y, Wen J, Phillips G, Shorten PR, McMahon CD, Wake GC, Chan WH, Thomas MF, Ren A, Moon S, Liu DX | title = Cyclic glycine-proline regulates IGF-1 homeostasis by altering the binding of IGFBP-3 to IGF-1 | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 4 | issue = 1 | article-number = 4388 | date = March 2014 | pmid = 24633053 | pmc = 3955921 | doi = 10.1038/srep04388 | bibcode = 2014NatSR...4.4388G | author-link7 = Jingyuan Wen | author-link2 = Peter Gluckman }}</ref>

Research shows that cGP can normalize IGF-1 function under pathophysiological conditions of increased or diminished IGF-1 bioactivity.<ref name="Guan Gluckman Yang et al 2014"/>

In vitro studies show that cGP promoted the activity of IGF-1 when insufficient and inhibited the activity of IGF-1 when in excess.<ref name="Guan Gluckman Yang et al 2014"/>

== Pharmacology ==

=== Pharmacodynamics ===
The [[mechanism of action]] of traneurocin is either unknown or undisclosed.<ref name="DalviDewanganDas2020">{{cite journal | vauthors = Dalvi T, Dewangan B, Das R, Rani J, Shinde SD, Vhora N, Jain A, Sahu B | title = Old Drugs with New Tricks: Paradigm in Drug Development Pipeline for Alzheimer's Disease | journal = Central Nervous System Agents in Medicinal Chemistry | volume = 20 | issue = 3 | pages = 157–176 | date = 2020 | pmid = 33087034 | doi = 10.2174/1871524920666201021164805 }}</ref><ref name="CummingsLeeRitter2019">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cummings J, Lee G, Ritter A, Sabbagh M, Zhong K | title = Alzheimer's disease drug development pipeline: 2019 | journal = Alzheimer's & Dementia | volume = 5 | issue = 1 | pages = 272–293 | year = 2019 | pmid = 31334330 | pmc = 6617248 | doi = 10.1016/j.trci.2019.05.008 | publisher = Wiley | doi-access = free }}</ref> However, it has been described as acting as a [[positive allosteric modulator]] of the [[AMPA receptor]] and has been found to increase [[brain-derived neurotrophic factor]] (BDNF) levels.<ref name="AdisInsight" /><ref name="AlzForum">{{cite web | title=NA-831 | website=ALZFORUM | date=28 November 2023 | url=https://www.alzforum.org/therapeutics/na-831 | access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref><ref name="GudashevaGrigorievKoliasnikova2016" /><ref name="GudashevaKoliasnikovaAntipova2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gudasheva TA, Koliasnikova KN, Antipova TA, Seredenin SB | title = Neuropeptide cycloprolylglycine increases the levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor in neuronal cells | journal = Doklady. Biochemistry and Biophysics | volume = 469 | issue = 1 | pages = 273–276 | date = July 2016 | pmid = 27599510 | doi = 10.1134/S1607672916040104 }}</ref> It has also been found to act as a positive allosteric modulator of the [[GABAA receptor|GABA<sub>A</sub> receptor]].<ref name="SharanovaBukanovaGudasheva2019">{{cite journal | vauthors = Sharonova IN, Bukanova YV, Gudasheva TA, Skrebitsky VG | title = Effect of Endogenous Neuropeptide Cycloprolylglycine on GABA<sub>A</sub> Receptors in Cerebellar Purkinje Cells | journal = Bulletin of Experimental Biology and Medicine | volume = 167 | issue = 1 | pages = 39–42 | date = May 2019 | pmid = 31177457 | doi = 10.1007/s10517-019-04455-7 }}</ref> The drug is described as having [[neuroprotective]], [[neurogenesis|neurogenesis-stimulating]], and [[nootropic|pro-cognitive or nootropic]] effects.<ref name="AlavianKolahdouzanMortezazadeh2021">{{cite journal | vauthors = Alavian G, Kolahdouzan K, Mortezazadeh M, Torabi ZS | title = Antiretrovirals for Prophylaxis Against COVID-19: A Comprehensive Literature Review | journal = Journal of Clinical Pharmacology | volume = 61 | issue = 5 | pages = 581–590 | date = May 2021 | pmid = 33217030 | pmc = 7753707 | doi = 10.1002/jcph.1788 }}</ref><ref name="AlipourMahmoudiAhmadi2023">{{cite journal | vauthors = Alipour S, Mahmoudi L, Ahmadi F | title = Pulmonary drug delivery: an effective and convenient delivery route to combat COVID-19 | journal = Drug Delivery and Translational Research | volume = 13 | issue = 3 | pages = 705–715 | date = March 2023 | pmid = 36260223 | pmc = 9580423 | doi = 10.1007/s13346-022-01251-1 }}</ref><ref name="ChoiChoiKopp2024">{{cite journal | vauthors = Choi HS, Choi AY, Kopp JB, Winkler CA, Cho SK | title = Review of COVID-19 Therapeutics by Mechanism: From Discovery to Approval | journal = Journal of Korean Medical Science | volume = 39 | issue = 14 | article-number = e134 | date = April 2024 | pmid = 38622939 | pmc = 11018982 | doi = 10.3346/jkms.2024.39.e134 }}</ref><ref name="TranTranVu2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Tran B, Tran L, Vu F | title=P4-202: NA-831 as a Regenerative Therapeutic for Alzheimer's Disease: A Phase 1 Safety, Tolerability and Pharmacokinetics Study | journal=Alzheimer's & Dementia | publisher=Wiley | volume=14 | issue=7S_Part_29 | year=2018 | issn=1552-5260 | doi=10.1016/j.jalz.2018.07.023 | page=}}</ref><ref name="GudashevaGrigorievKoliasnikova2016" /> It has also been reported to have [[Hypoxia (medical)|antihypoxic]] and [[anxiolytic]] properties.<ref name="Gudasheva2015" /><ref name="GudashevaGrigorievKoliasnikova2016" />

=== Pharmacokinetics ===
It is known to be an [[endogenous]] [[chemical compound|compound]] present at [[micromolar]] concentrations in the rat [[brain]] and readily crosses the [[blood–brain barrier]].<ref name="TranTranVu2018" /><ref name="GudashevaGrigorievKoliasnikova2016" />

== Chemistry ==

Chemically, traneurocin is a [[synthetic compound|synthetic]] [[cyclic compound|cyclized]] [[dipeptide]] composed of the [[amino acid]]s [[glycine]] and [[proline]].<ref name="Synapse" /><ref name="DrugBank">{{cite web | title=Cyclo(prolylglycyl): Uses, Interactions, Mechanism of Action | website=DrugBank Online | date=13 June 2005 | url=https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB04541 | access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref><ref name="PubChem">{{cite web | title=(S)-Hexahydropyrrolo[1,2-a]pyrazine-1,4-dione | website=PubChem | url=https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/126154 | access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref>

== Potential uses ==
Biologically, cGP is most strongly associated with cognitive benefits, however it also has a role in other biological functions, as outlined below.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hu L, Lin J, Qin F, Xu L, Luo L | title = Exploring Sources, Biological Functions, and Potential Applications of the Ubiquitous Marine Cyclic Dipeptide: A Concise Review of Cyclic Glycine-Proline | journal = Marine Drugs | volume = 22 | issue = 6 | page = 271 | date = June 2024 | pmid = 38921582 | pmc = 11205142 | doi = 10.3390/md22060271 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

=== Cognition ===
Vascular health is critical in maintaining cognitive function.<ref name="Age-related memory decline is assoc"/> IGF-1 plays an essential role in vascular remodelling of the brain and supports cognitive retention.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lopez-Lopez C, LeRoith D, Torres-Aleman I | title = Insulin-like growth factor I is required for vessel remodeling in the adult brain | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 101 | issue = 26 | pages = 9833–9838 | date = June 2004 | pmid = 15210967 | pmc = 470760 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.0400337101 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2004PNAS..101.9833L }}</ref> Metabolic IGF-1 levels tend to reduce with age and this reduction appears to be a major contributor to cognitive impairment in older populations.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Okereke OI, Kang JH, Ma J, Gaziano JM, Grodstein F | title = Midlife plasma insulin-like growth factor I and cognitive function in older men | journal = The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism | volume = 91 | issue = 11 | pages = 4306–4312 | date = November 2006 | pmid = 16912125 | doi = 10.1210/jc.2006-1325 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Okereke O, Kang JH, Ma J, Hankinson SE, Pollak MN, Grodstein F | title = Plasma IGF-I levels and cognitive performance in older women | journal = Neurobiology of Aging | volume = 28 | issue = 1 | pages = 135–142 | date = January 2007 | pmid = 16337715 | doi = 10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2005.10.012 | s2cid = 44509810 }}</ref>

Low or deficient IGF-1 levels can be normalized by cGP, restoring its vascular function.<ref name="Guan Gluckman Yang et al 2014"/> Studies evaluating cGP, IGF-1 and IGFBP3 levels suggest that cGP concentration and cGP/IGF-1 molar ratio were positively associated suggesting that older people with higher plasma cGP concentration (and cGP/IGF-1 molar ratio) have better memory/cognitive retention.<ref name="Fan Pitcher Dalrymple‐Alford et al 2020"/>

=== Hypertension ===
IGF-1 plays a critical role in energy metabolism with deficient IGF-1 levels being implicated in obesity and hypertension.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Karmali R, Dalovisio A, Borgia JA, Venugopal P, Kim BW, Grant-Szymanski K, Hari P, Lazarus H | title = All in the family: Clueing into the link between metabolic syndrome and hematologic malignancies | journal = Blood Reviews | volume = 29 | issue = 2 | pages = 71–80 | date = March 2015 | pmid = 25433571 | doi = 10.1016/j.blre.2014.09.010 }}</ref>

=== Stroke ===
The role of IGF-1 in supporting recovery from stroke, which is a condition of vascular origin, is reported.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sierra C, Coca A, Schiffrin EL | title = Vascular mechanisms in the pathogenesis of stroke | journal = Current Hypertension Reports | volume = 13 | issue = 3 | pages = 200–207 | date = June 2011 | pmid = 21331606 | doi = 10.1007/s11906-011-0195-x | s2cid = 13442699 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Guan J, Bennet L, Gluckman PD, Gunn AJ | title = Insulin-like growth factor-1 and post-ischemic brain injury | journal = Progress in Neurobiology | volume = 70 | issue = 6 | pages = 443–462 | date = August 2003 | pmid = 14568359 | doi = 10.1016/j.pneurobio.2003.08.002 | s2cid = 12719687 }}</ref> A study in 34 stroke patients reported that patients with higher plasma concentration of cGP made better recovery within 3 months than those with lower cGP levels. Further, patients with higher cGP levels also showed lesser neurological deficits.<ref name="Fan Pitcher Dalrymple‐Alford et al 2020"/>

=== Therapeutic potential ===
Excessive IGF-1 activity promotes tumorigenesis<ref name="Shanmugalingam Bosco Ridley et al 2016"/> while reduced IGF-1 activity is linked with diseases such as Alzheimer's disease<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kang D, Waldvogel HJ, Wang A, Fan D, Faull RL, Curtis MA, Shorten PR, Guan J | title = The autocrine regulation of insulin-like growth factor-1 in human brain of Alzheimer's disease | journal = Psychoneuroendocrinology | volume = 127 | article-number = 105191 | date = May 2021 | pmid = 33706042 | doi = 10.1016/j.psyneuen.2021.105191 | s2cid = 232116896 }}</ref> and Parkinson's disease.<ref name="Fan Pitcher Dalrymple‐Alford et al 2020"/> cGP normalises the autocrine function of IGF-1 under pathological conditions and when there are low levels of cGP in the human body, IGF-1 regulation is compromised.<ref name="Guan Gluckman Yang et al 2014"/> Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that treatment with exogenous cGP could assist with improving IGF-1 implicated health benefits.<ref name="LTran-patent-7232798"/>

== Clinical trials ==
As of September 2024, traneurocin is in [[Phases of clinical research#Phase III|phase 3]] [[clinical trial]]s for COVID-19, [[Phases of clinical research#Phase II|phase 2]] clinical trials for Alzheimer's disease,<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03538522 |title=A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study to Assess the Safety, Tolerability, and Efficacy of NA-831 in Alzheimer Patients With Mild Cognitive Impairment |last=Biomed Industries, Inc. |date=2020-06-26 |publisher=clinicaltrials.gov |issue=NCT03538522}}</ref> fragile X syndrome, and Rett syndrome, and [[Phases of clinical research#Phase I|phase 1]] clinical trials for major depressive disorder.<ref name="AdisInsight" /> No development has been reported for treatment of other neurological disorders.<ref name="AdisInsight" /> Traneurocin was first developed, under the name cycloprolylglycine (CPG), in [[Russia]] in 1991 as a drug related [[chemical structure|structurally]] and [[pharmacology|pharmacologically]] to [[piracetam]].<ref name="Gudasheva2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gudasheva TA | title=Theoretical grounds and technologies for dipeptide drug development | journal=Russian Chemical Bulletin | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=64 | issue=9 | year=2015 | issn=1066-5285 | doi=10.1007/s11172-015-1112-2 | pages=2012–2021}}</ref><ref name="GudashevaGrigorievKoliasnikova2016" /><ref name="GudashevaVasilevichZolotov1991">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gudasheva TA, Vasilevich NI, Zolotov NN, Lezina VP, Rozenberg SG, Kravchenko EV, Ostrovskaya RU, Voronina TA, Rozantsev GG, Skoldinov AP | title = Mechanism of nootropic effect of topological proline-based piracetam analogues. | journal = Khim.-Farm. Zh. | date = 1991 | volume = 25 | issue = 6 | pages = 12–16 | url = https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=3952160753610416095}}</ref> Cycloprolylglycine is also related to and known to be the major [[metabolite]] of [[omberacetam]] (Noopept).<ref name="Gudasheva2015" />

Another drug, [[vineurocin]] (NA-704), is also being developed for treatment of Alzheimer's disease.<ref name="AdisInsight-Vineurocin">{{cite web | title=Vineurocine | work = AdisInsight | publisher = Springer Nature Switzerland AG | date=7 April 2021 | url=https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800051886 | access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref><ref name="Synapse-Vineurocin">{{cite web | title=Delving into the Latest Updates on Vineurocin with Synapse | website=Synapse | date=28 September 2024 | url=https://synapse.patsnap.com/drug/b410f62c2730498c9a2d32bb588a8218 | access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref> This drug is described as a [[recombinant protein|recombinant]] [[growth hormone]] with neuroprotective and neurogenic effects.<ref name="SachsForum2017">{{cite web | title=1st NIF Presenting Companies | website=SachsForum | date=18 September 2017 | url=https://www.sachsforum.com/nif-presenters.html | access-date=19 October 2024 | quote=2. Our second drug candidate, Vineurocin (NA-704) is a recombinant human growth hormone that modulates the aging process in humans. NA-704 exhibits neuroprotection and neurogenesis, which has been demonstrated as a strong candidate for treatment of Alzheimer's disease and other neurological disorders. The NA-704 Phase 2 will be from June 2018 to May 2019.}}</ref>

Cyclic glycine-proline (cGP) is a small neuroactive peptide that belongs to a group of bioactive 2,5-diketopiperazines (2,5-DKPs) and is also known as cyclo-glycine-proline. cGP is a neutral, stable naturally occurring compound and is endogenous to the human body; found in human plasma, breast milk and cerebrospinal fluid.  DKPs are bioactive compounds often found in foods. Cyclic dipeptides such as 2,5 DKPs are formed by the cyclisation of two amino acids of linear peptides produced in heated or fermented foods. The bioactivity of cGP is a property of functional foods and presents in several matrices of foods including blackcurrants.
cGP is metabolite of hormone insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). It has a cyclic structure, lipophilic nature, and is enzymatically stable which makes its a more favorable candidate for manipulating the binding-release process between IGF-1 and its binding protein thereby, normalizing IGF-1 function.
Under the trade name Traneurocin (developmental code name NA-831), it is being developed as a racetam-like drug for the treatment of COVID-19, Alzheimer's disease, fragile X syndrome, Rett syndrome, major depressive disorder, and other neurological disorders. In the case of COVID-19, it is specifically being developed for treatment of COVID-19-induced neuropathy.
